new_statements.quote: Finally, stress in Nyiyaparli is typical for an Australian language. Primary stress almost always falls on the first syllable of a word, characterised by an increase in loudness. Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed. The examples in (2.3) illustrate this pattern. (2.3) a. "kanti,purrku 'mob' ... b. "intin,malpi 'rain-PST' ... c. "thungku,wayi,laka,lay 'cooked-INCH-when' ... d. "nyupa,ngarni,thakuru 'spouse-PROP-CAUS-SIM=now'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of PDF p. 26 = thesis p. 14, section 2.4 Phonotactics). The prose is there word for word: 'Finally, stress in Nyiyaparli is typical for an Australian language. Primary stress almost always falls on the first syllable of a word, characterised by an increase in loudness. Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed. The examples in (2.3) illustrate this pattern.' followed by (2.3a-d) kantipurrku 'mob', intinmalpi 'rain-PST', thungkuwayilakalay 'cooked-INCH-when', nyupangarnithakuru 'spouse-PROP-CAUS-SIM=now' with primary-stress mark on syllable 1 and secondary marks on s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (impressionistic cue: loudness); secondary stresses on subsequent odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th,...), i.e. left-to-right trochaic alternation; a final odd syllable may optionally go unstressed (no obligatory final secondary stress). Not weight-sensitive; not tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed.' Examples mark secondary stress on syllables 3 (and 5, 7) of 4-, 5- and 7-syllable words, including across suffix/clitic boundaries (thungku-wayi-laka-lay, nyupa-ngarni-thakuru).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged 'almost always' for initial primary stress, no specific exceptions listed; optional non-stressing of a word-final odd syllable. Author notes phonology is treated only briefly as background to morphosyntax; stress description is impressionistic (no acoustic study of stress; the thesis's small acoustic study concerns vowels).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (grammatical/phonological) word including suffixes and enclitics, as the examples show secondary stress counted continuously across nominal suffixes, verbal inflections and the =lay clitic; examples drawn from connected narrative recordings (von Brandenstein 1960s tapes, Battin 2019 fieldwork), not citation forms specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Battin 2019 describes Nyiyaparli as spoken by Nyiyaparli and Palyku people and treats Nyiyaparli and Palyku as varieties of one language ('Nyiyaparli/Palyku'), matching Glottolog's language-level node nija1241 'Nyiyaparli-Palyku' (ISO xny). Data come mainly from Gordon Mackay (von Brandenstein recordings, 1960s) and David Stock (2019); Battin notes some variation between speakers may be dialectal but does not assign the stress description to one dialect. The ANU repository records the work as an Honours thesis (Glottolog lists it as a masters thesis).
